UPPER GI__Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Dise:
Overview

GORD: reflux of gastric contents through an incompetent lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) → acid irritates the oesophageal squamous mucosa → inflammation, erosion, and metaplasia.

Why the Oesophagus is Vulnerable

Oesophagus = squamous epithelium → acid-sensitive
Stomach = columnar epithelium → acid-resistant
Chronic acid exposure drives the squamous → columnar metaplasia of Barrett's oesophagus.

The Central Fork

Typical symptoms + no red flags → empirical treatment (no investigation needed)
ALARM red flags present → OGD first

💡 Cross-references: Dyspepsia (GORD is a cause) · Achalasia (mimics reflux; different dysphagia pattern + manometry) · PUD/H. pylori (shared acid-suppression management)
Causes & Triggers
↑ Intra-abdominal Pressure / LOS Incompetence
  • Hiatus hernia — most common structural cause
  • Obesity
  • Pregnancy
LOS-Relaxing / Irritant Factors
  • Alcohol, smoking
  • Coffee/tea, fatty or spicy foods
  • NSAIDs
  • Stress, large late meals
Clinical Features
Typical
  • Heartburn — retrosternal burning, worse lying flat, bending forward, post-meal
  • Acid regurgitation — sour taste in mouth
  • Retrosternal / epigastric pain
  • Bloating, belching
Atypical (Often Missed)
  • Nocturnal cough
  • Hoarseness (laryngopharyngeal reflux)
  • Dental erosion
  • Asthma-like wheeze
⚠ GORD vs Achalasia: GORD = burning + regurgitation. If dysphagia is the dominant symptom → red flag. Think obstruction (cancer) or motility disorder (achalasia), not simple GORD.
Investigations
📋 GORD is a clinical diagnosis. Most patients are treated empirically without investigation. OGD is reserved for those with ALARM red flags.
ALARM Red Flags → Urgent OGD
Letter Red Flag
AAnaemia (iron deficiency)
LLoss of weight
AAnorexia
RRecent onset / progressive symptoms
MMelaena / haematemesis
Plus: Dysphagia · Age >55 with new dyspepsia · Persistent (>4 weeks) or relapsing symptoms despite treatment
🔭
OGD (Endoscopy)
First-line if ALARM flags present. Visualises oesophagitis grade, Barrett's metaplasia, or malignancy. Allows biopsy.
📊
24h pH Monitoring
If OGD negative but symptoms persist. pH <4 for >4% of time = pathological acid reflux confirmed. ± impedance testing.
📋
Oesophageal Manometry
Measures LOS pressure. Essential for achalasia diagnosis. Pre-operative assessment before fundoplication.
Management
🏃
Conservative — All Patients
Weight loss · Smoking cessation · ↓ alcohol · Avoid trigger foods (coffee, fatty/spicy) · Smaller, earlier meals · Raise head of bed · Antacids / alginates ("foam raft") for mild symptoms
↓ endoscopy-proven oesophagitis
💊
Endoscopy-Proven Oesophagitis
Full-dose PPI 1–2 months → responds: step down to lowest effective dose · no response: double-dose PPI 1 month
↓ endoscopy-negative reflux
💊
Endoscopy-Negative Reflux
Full-dose PPI 1 month → responds: low dose · no response: H2RA (famotidine) or prokinetic (metoclopramide, domperidone)
↓ refractory / severe
🔪
Laparoscopic Fundoplication
Wraps the gastric fundus around the LOS to mechanically reinforce it. For refractory disease or patients who prefer surgery over lifelong medication.
PPIs — Mechanism & Long-Term Side Effects
Mechanism

Irreversibly block H⁺/K⁺ ATPase (proton pump) on gastric parietal cells → suppress acid secretion. Examples: omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole.

Long-term Side Effects (Examinable)
  • Hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia
  • Osteoporosis / fractures
  • C. difficile risk
  • Microscopic colitis
  • ↓ Vitamin B12 absorption
Barrett's Oesophagus

Definition: chronic acid exposure → lower oesophageal squamous → columnar metaplasia (an adaptive response). Premalignant — can progress to oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

⭐ The stepwise progression to memorise:
GORD → Barrett's (metaplasia) → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma
This pathway is the single highest-yield SBA object in the topic.
Risk Factors for Barrett's
  • Chronic GORD
  • Male sex
  • Smoking
  • Central obesity
Management
  • High-dose PPI (acid suppression)
  • Metaplasia only → endoscopic surveillance + biopsy every 3–5 years
  • Low-grade dysplasia → surveillance or RFA
  • High-grade dysplasia → radiofrequency ablation (RFA) 1st-line; endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) if nodular
💡 Cancer type split (cross-ref Oesophageal Cancer):
Barrett's / GORD / obesity → adenocarcinoma (lower 1/3)
Smoking / alcohol / achalasia / iron deficiency → squamous cell carcinoma (upper/middle 1/3)
⭐ Exam Pearls
GORD = clinical diagnosis. Treat empirically unless ALARM red flags → then OGD.
ALARM: Anaemia · weiLght Loss · Anorexia · Recent/progressive · Melaena/haematemesis · + dysphagia · age >55 new-onset → urgent endoscopy.
PPIs irreversibly block H⁺/K⁺ ATPase. Long-term: hypomagnesaemia, hyponatraemia, osteoporosis, C. diff, ↓B12.
Negative OGD + ongoing symptoms → 24h pH monitoring (the confirmatory test).
Barrett's = squamous→columnar metaplasia → adenocarcinoma. Metaplasia: surveillance. Dysplasia: RFA.
Cancer split: GORD/Barrett's/obesity → adeno; smoking/alcohol/achalasia → squamous.
Refractory GORD → laparoscopic fundoplication.
UPPER GI__Dyspepsia:
Overview

Dyspepsia is a symptom complex, not a diagnosis: epigastric pain/discomfort, fullness, early satiety, heartburn, bloating, nausea. It is an umbrella term — the note is fundamentally about triaging the differential beneath it.

Causes Beneath the Umbrella
  • Functional dyspepsia — commonest; normal OGD
  • GORD — heartburn, regurgitation
  • PUD / H. pylori — epigastric pain, meal relation
  • Gastric cancer — red flags
  • Drug-induced — NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, steroids
The Central Fork

Red flags present → endoscopy / urgent referral
No red flags → empirical management (PPI or H. pylori test-and-treat)

This triage question is the whole topic.

💡 Dyspepsia vs GORD: Dyspepsia is epigastric-centred (stomach pattern — fullness, pain, nausea). GORD is retrosternal burning + acid regurgitation (reflux pattern). GORD sits under the dyspepsia umbrella but is a distinct entity.
⭐ Referral Criteria (The Central Decision Object)

Frame this as three tiers: urgent 2WW → non-urgent → empirical. The unifying logic is the ALARM features + dysphagia + age ≥55.

🚨 Urgent (2-Week-Wait) Endoscopy
🔴
Dysphagia
Any age — the single strongest red flag. Scope now regardless of other features.
🔴
Upper Abdominal Mass
Consistent with gastric cancer. 2WW at any age.
🔴
Age ≥55 + Weight Loss + Upper-GI Symptom
Upper abdominal pain, reflux, or dyspepsia in combination with age ≥55 and weight loss = 2WW.
🟡 Non-Urgent Endoscopy Referral
Criterion Detail
HaematemesisAny age
Age ≥55 + treatment-resistant dyspepsiaFailed empirical therapy
Age ≥55 + upper abdo pain + low HbIron-deficiency anaemia + pain
Raised platelets (thrombocytosis) + upper-GI symptomNausea / vomiting / weight loss / reflux / dyspepsia / abdo pain — newer red flag, frequently missed
Age ≥55 + nausea/vomiting + upper-GI symptomWeight loss / reflux / dyspepsia / upper abdo pain
⭐ ALARM red flags (same set as GORD): Anaemia · weight Loss · Anorexia · Recent progressive symptoms · Melaena/haematemesis — plus dysphagia and age ≥55. Dysphagia + abdominal mass = "scope now"; the rest stratify urgency.
Management — No Red Flags (Empirical Pathway)
💊
Step 1 — Review Medications
Identify iatrogenic cause: NSAIDs (most common), bisphosphonates, steroids, calcium antagonists, iron. Stop/switch if possible.
↓
🏃
Step 2 — Lifestyle Advice
Weight loss · ↓ alcohol and smoking · Avoid trigger foods · Smaller, earlier meals (shared with GORD advice)
↓
🔀
Step 3 — First-Line: PPI or Test-and-Treat (choose one)
Either is acceptable first-line. If one fails → switch to the other.
Option A — Full-Dose PPI (1 month)

Omeprazole / lansoprazole for 1 month. Responds → step down to lowest effective dose. No response → switch to H. pylori test-and-treat.

Option B — H. pylori Test-and-Treat

Urea breath test or stool antigen test → eradicate if positive (triple therapy). No response or H. pylori negative → switch to full-dose PPI.

⚠ Stop PPI for 2 weeks before H. pylori testing. PPIs suppress H. pylori activity → false negative on breath/stool tests. A classic SBA trap.
Differential Beneath the Umbrella
Cause Pointer Cross-ref
Functional dyspepsiaCommonest; normal OGD—
GORDHeartburn, regurgitationGORD note
PUD / H. pyloriEpigastric pain, relation to mealsPUD note
Gastric cancerRed flags: weight loss, mass, anaemia, dysphagia, age ≥55Gastric Cancer note
Drug-inducedNSAIDs most common; bisphosphonates, steroidsReview meds first
⭐ Exam Pearls
Dyspepsia = a symptom to triage, not a disease. The fork: red flags → refer/scope; no red flags → empirical.
Dysphagia or abdominal mass = urgent 2WW at any age. Age ≥55 + weight loss + upper-GI symptom = 2WW.
ALARM: Anaemia · weight Loss · Anorexia · Recent progressive · Melaena/haematemesis — + dysphagia + age ≥55.
No red flags → review meds + lifestyle → PPI 1 month OR H. pylori test-and-treat; switch if one fails.
Stop PPI 2 weeks before H. pylori testing — suppression causes false negatives.
Thrombocytosis (raised platelets) is a recognised red flag for upper-GI cancer — often missed.
Commonest cause = functional dyspepsia (normal endoscopy). Always cross-ref GORD, PUD, and Gastric Cancer.
UPPER GI__Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) and:
Overview

Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD): a break in the gastroduodenal mucosa extending down to the muscularis mucosae. Occurs when aggressive factors overwhelm the mucosal defence.

↑ Aggressive Factors
  • Gastric acid, pepsin
  • H. pylori (disrupts barrier)
  • NSAIDs (↓ prostaglandins → ↓ mucus)
  • Stress, smoking, alcohol, caffeine
  • Zollinger-Ellison (gastrinoma → massive acid)
↓ Mucosal Defences
  • Mucus–bicarbonate layer
  • Prostaglandin-mediated epithelial repair
  • Mucosal blood flow

Eradicate H. pylori and/or stop NSAIDs → most ulcers heal.

💡 Cross-references: Dyspepsia (PUD sits beneath that umbrella; shares test-and-treat) · GORD (shared PPI toolkit) · Gastric Cancer (GUs must always be biopsied)
⭐ Gastric vs Duodenal Ulcer Discriminator

The most testable clinical point — pain's relationship to food:

Gastric Ulcer Duodenal Ulcer
Frequency Less common More common
Pain vs food Worse with eating Relieved by eating; worse when hungry (esp. at night)
Weight Loss (fear of eating) Stable / gain (eats to relieve pain)
Malignancy Must biopsy — can be malignant Rarely malignant
⭐ Mnemonic: "Gastric = Greater with food; Duodenal = Decreased with food (Delayed pain when hungry)." Near-guaranteed SBA.
Clinical Features
🔥
Epigastric Pain
Pattern varies by ulcer type (see above). Associated nausea, bloating, dyspepsia.
🩸
Upper-GI Bleed
Haematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, melaena. Hypotension, tachycardia, ↓Hb. Commonest emergency complication.
💉
Chronic Anaemia
Microscopic bleeding → iron-deficiency anaemia (↓Hb, ↓MCV, ↓ferritin). May be the presenting feature.
💡 Drugs that ↑ bleeding risk: NSAIDs · aspirin · DOACs · steroids · SSRIs. Always review the drug chart.
Investigations
💨
H. pylori Testing (non-invasive)
Age <55 + no red flags. Urea breath test or stool antigen test. Stop PPI 2 weeks + antibiotics 4 weeks before.
🔭
OGD (Endoscopy)
Age ≥55 or red flags. Visualises ulcer, allows biopsy. All GUs biopsied. GUs repeated at 6–8 weeks to confirm healing.
🩺
Bloods
FBC (anaemia), U&E, LFTs, coagulation, G&S (if bleeding). Urea often raised disproportionately in upper-GI bleed (digestion of blood).
🫁
Erect CXR (if perforation suspected)
Air under the diaphragm = pneumoperitoneum = perforation until proven otherwise.
⭐ All gastric ulcers must be biopsied AND have repeat OGD at 6–8 weeks to confirm healing (exclude malignancy). Duodenal ulcers are rarely malignant — this rule does not apply.
Management
H. pylori Positive
  • Eradication therapy (see H. pylori section below)
  • PPI for ulcer healing
  • GUs: repeat OGD at 6–8 weeks
  • Confirm eradication with urea breath test
H. pylori Negative
  • Stop the cause — review/stop NSAIDs
  • Full-dose PPI for healing
  • GUs: repeat OGD to confirm healing
  • Gastroprotection if NSAID cannot be stopped
🚨 Acute Bleeding Ulcer
🔴
Resuscitate
IV access · fluids · cross-match · correct coagulopathy · Hb target ≥70 g/L (restrictive transfusion)
↓
💊
IV PPI
High-dose IV PPI (omeprazole/pantoprazole) — reduces rebleed risk
↓
🔭
Urgent OGD + Endoscopic Intervention (1st-line)
Adrenaline injection · thermal coagulation · haemostatic clips
Complications
🩸
Bleeding
Commonest, most life-threatening. Haematemesis, melaena. Endoscopic haemostasis 1st-line; interventional radiology or surgery if refractory.
💥
Perforation
Acute abdomen + peritonitis. Erect CXR → air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). Emergency surgical repair.
🚫
Gastric Outlet Obstruction
Pyloric scarring/stricture → early satiety, distension, projectile vomiting → metabolic alkalosis (loss of H⁺ + Cl⁻). Balloon dilatation or surgery.
Acute Erosive & Stress-Related Gastritis

Gastritis = inflammation of the gastric mucosa without a full-thickness mucosal break — the step before an ulcer (contrast PUD, which reaches the muscularis mucosae). Same aggressive drivers as PUD: H. pylori, NSAIDs, alcohol, and physiological stress.

Chronic gastritis — two classic types
  • Type B (antral) — H. pylori: commonest; antrum; → PUD + gastric cancer / MALT lymphoma
  • Type A (fundal) — autoimmune: anti-parietal cell / anti-IF antibodies → ↓ acid + ↓ IF → pernicious anaemia + gastric cancer risk (cross-ref B12 anaemia)
Acute erosive / haemorrhagic gastritis
  • NSAIDs, alcohol, severe physiological stress
  • Superficial erosions → can cause an upper-GI bleed (gastritis / duodenitis ≈ 8% of upper bleeds)
🚨 Stress ulcers — the two named eponyms
Curling's ulcer

Severe burns → hypovolaemia → gastric mucosal ischaemia. (Curling ↔ the flame.)

Cushing's ulcer

Head injury / raised ICP / CNS insult → vagal overstimulation → ↑↑ acid. (Cushing ↔ the brain.)

⭐ Stress ulcer prophylaxis (PPI or H2-blocker) for the critically ill at highest risk: major burns, head injury, mechanical ventilation for over 48 h, coagulopathy. Curling's = burns; Cushing's = CNS / head injury — a near-guaranteed SBA pairing.
Helicobacter pylori

Gram-negative spiral bacterium colonising the gastric antrum. The single most important cause of PUD. Also associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.

Survival Mechanisms
  • Urease — splits urea → ammonia → neutralises local acid
  • CagA cytotoxin — mucosal damage, inflammation
  • Flagella — burrows into the protective mucus layer
Associations
  • Peptic ulcer disease (gastric + duodenal)
  • Gastric adenocarcinoma
  • MALT lymphoma — eradication can induce remission
Testing
💨
Urea Breath Test
Urease splits 13C-labelled urea → labelled CO₂ detected on exhalation. Also used to confirm eradication post-treatment.
💩
Stool Antigen Test
Non-invasive. Also confirms eradication. Equally valid alternative to breath test.
🔬
CLO (Rapid Urease) Test
On OGD biopsy sample from gastric antrum. Urease activity changes pH indicator colour. Invasive but immediate result.
⚠ Stop PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics 4 weeks before H. pylori testing — both suppress bacterial activity → false negative. High-yield SBA trap.
Eradication — 7-Day Triple Therapy
First-Line

PPI + Amoxicillin + Clarithromycin — 7 days

Penicillin-Allergic

PPI + Metronidazole + Clarithromycin — 7 days

💡 Confirm eradication with urea breath test or stool antigen (especially if complicated disease or symptoms persist).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Fork: ↑acid vs ↓mucosal barrier. Two treatable causes: H. pylori + NSAIDs.
GU = pain worse with food + weight loss; DU = pain relieved by food, worse when hungry (and commoner).
All GUs biopsied + repeat OGD at 6–8 weeks to confirm healing (exclude cancer). DUs don't need this.
H. pylori: urease (survives acid), CagA (mucosal damage), flagella (burrows in mucus). Associated with PUD, gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma.
Stop PPI 2 weeks + antibiotics 4 weeks before H. pylori testing → false negatives otherwise.
Eradication: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin (7 days); metronidazole if penicillin-allergic. Confirm with urea breath test.
Perforation → erect CXR → air under diaphragm. Outlet obstruction → projectile vomiting → metabolic alkalosis.
Bleeding ulcer → IV PPI + urgent OGD + endoscopic haemostasis. Bleeding risk ↑: NSAIDs, aspirin, DOACs, steroids, SSRIs.
Zollinger-Ellison (gastrinoma ± MEN1) = refractory/multiple ulcers, high acid. MALT lymphoma may remit with H. pylori eradication alone.
Stress ulcers: Curling's = burns (mucosal ischaemia); Cushing's = head injury / raised ICP (vagal → ↑ acid). Prophylax the critically ill (PPI/H2): burns, head injury, ventilation >48 h, coagulopathy.
Gastritis = mucosal inflammation without a break (vs PUD). Type B = H. pylori (antrum); Type A = autoimmune (fundus → pernicious anaemia). Acute erosive gastritis (NSAIDs/alcohol/stress) can bleed.
UPPER GI__Gastric Cancer:
Overview

Gastric cancer: >90% adenocarcinoma, mostly arising in the antrum. A leading cause of cancer death worldwide, with late presentation and poor prognosis.

⭐ The metaplasia pathway:
H. pylori → chronic inflammation → gastric atrophy → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma
This chain is the highest-yield mechanistic object in the topic.
💡 Cross-references: PUD / H. pylori (same organism — three diseases: PUD, gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma) · Oesophageal cancer (shared staging, surgery/palliation logic, Virchow's) · Pernicious anaemia / B12 (risk factor + post-gastrectomy complication)
Risk Factors
Major (H. pylori Pathway)
  • H. pylori — dominant cause (~6× risk); drives the metaplasia chain
  • Pernicious anaemia / atrophic gastritis — autoimmune; loss of parietal cells → metaplasia risk (cross-ref B12)
  • Commonest in Japan / Far East (high H. pylori prevalence + dietary factors)
Other Risk Factors
  • Male sex, increasing age
  • Smoking, alcohol
  • Salt-preserved / smoked diet
  • Family history, blood group A
💡 One bug, three diseases: H. pylori → PUD (ulceration) + gastric adenocarcinoma (metaplasia chain) + MALT lymphoma (eradication can induce remission).
Clinical Features

Symptoms are late and non-specific — the primary reason for poor prognosis. Red-flag vigilance in dyspepsia exists precisely because of this.

🔥
Dyspepsia
New-onset or PPI-resistant dyspepsia in age ≥55 = red flag. Early satiety, nausea, epigastric discomfort.
⚖️
Weight Loss + Anorexia
Cancer cachexia. Usually present by the time of diagnosis. A core 2WW trigger.
🍽️
Dysphagia / Vomiting
Cardia tumours → dysphagia. Pyloric tumours → gastric outlet obstruction, projectile vomiting.
🩸
Anaemia / Melaena
Chronic occult bleeding → iron-deficiency anaemia. Frank melaena = ulcerated tumour.
⭐ Eponymous Metastatic Signs (High-Yield)
Sign Location Significance
Virchow's node (Troisier's sign) Left supraclavicular lymph node Metastatic spread via thoracic duct
Sister Mary Joseph nodule Periumbilical nodule Peritoneal metastasis via ligamentum teres
Krukenberg tumour Ovarian metastasis Signet-ring cell mets to ovary; bilateral
Acanthosis nigricans Axillae / skin folds Paraneoplastic sign — velvety hyperpigmentation
Investigations
🔭
OGD + Biopsy (2WW)
Primary investigation. Biopsy confirms histology, CLO test for H. pylori, HER2 expression (targeted therapy). Red-flag/2WW criteria same as dyspepsia/oesophageal cancer.
🖥️
CT Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis
Staging — local, regional, distant metastases. Followed by PET-CT if curative intent considered.
🔬
Staging Laparoscopy
Detects peritoneal metastases not visible on CT. Essential before committing to curative resection.
🩺
Bloods
FBC (IDA), U&E, LFTs (liver mets), coagulation, G&S, CEA/CA19-9 (tumour markers, limited utility).
⭐ Histological hallmarks:
Signet-ring cells — mucin vacuole displaces nucleus to periphery; classic gastric cancer cell
Linitis plastica — diffuse infiltration of the stomach wall → rigid "leather-bottle" stomach on barium/CT
Management
Curative Intent
💊
Perioperative Chemotherapy
4 cycles neoadjuvant (to downstage) + 4 cycles adjuvant. FLOT regimen (5-FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, docetaxel).
↓
🔪
Surgery — Gastrectomy
Proximal / total tumour → total gastrectomy; distal tumour → subtotal gastrectomy. Reconstruction: Roux-en-Y. Early T1a tumours → EMR (endoscopic mucosal resection).
Post-Gastrectomy Complications (High-Yield)
💥
Anastomotic Leak
Post-op deterioration = assume leak until proven otherwise — same rule as oesophagectomy. Sepsis, tachycardia, failure to progress. High mortality.
⚡
Dumping Syndrome
Early (~30 min): hypertonic chyme → fluid shift → distension, nausea, hypovolaemia.
Late (1–3h): reactive hypoglycaemia from insulin surge.
Rx: small frequent low-simple-carb meals; separate food from drink.
💉
B12 Deficiency
Loss of parietal cells → loss of intrinsic factor → cannot absorb B12. Requires lifelong 3-monthly B12 injections (cross-ref pernicious anaemia).
Palliative Intent
Systemic Therapy

Palliative chemotherapy (symptom control, tumour shrinkage). Trastuzumab (anti-HER2) if HER2-positive — targeted therapy.

Supportive

NG / RIG for nutritional support · stenting for outlet obstruction · palliative care MDT.

⭐ Exam Pearls
>90% adenocarcinoma. Pathway: H. pylori → metaplasia → dysplasia → adeno. Commonest in Japan/Far East.
One bug, three diseases: H. pylori → PUD + gastric adenocarcinoma + MALT lymphoma.
Eponymous mets: Virchow's/Troisier's (left supraclavicular) · Sister Mary Joseph (umbilical) · Krukenberg (ovary) · acanthosis nigricans.
Signet-ring cells = classic histology. Linitis plastica = diffuse infiltration = "leather-bottle" stomach.
OGD + biopsy (2WW); stage with CT + staging laparoscopy; check HER2 for trastuzumab eligibility.
Proximal → total gastrectomy; distal → subtotal; Roux-en-Y reconstruction. Early T1a → EMR.
Post-gastrectomy: dumping syndrome (early=fluid shift, late=hypoglycaemia) + B12 deficiency (3-monthly injections) + anastomotic leak.
Pernicious anaemia = precancerous (atrophic gastritis → metaplasia risk). Cross-ref B12 deficiency post-op.
UPPER GI__Oesophageal Cancer:
Overview

Two histological types — squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and adenocarcinoma — with distinct epidemiology, locations, risk factors, and treatment. Understanding which is which organises the entire topic.

🔴 Progressive dysphagia (solids → then liquids) = oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise. This is the mechanical dysphagia pattern — contrast with achalasia where dysphagia to liquids AND solids occurs simultaneously from the start (motility problem).
💡 Cross-references: GORD / Barrett's (the adenocarcinoma pathway) · Achalasia (risk factor for both types + the dysphagia discriminator) · Dyspepsia (shares the red-flag → 2WW OGD trigger)
⭐ SCC vs Adenocarcinoma — The Central Comparison
Squamous Cell Carcinoma Adenocarcinoma
Epidemiology Developing world Developed world (UK / US)
Location Upper / middle third Lower third (gastro-oesophageal junction)
Risk factors Smoking, alcohol, achalasia, iron deficiency (Plummer-Vinson), low vit A, hot drinks GORD, Barrett's oesophagus, obesity, smoking, achalasia, high-fat diet
Mechanism Chronic mucosal irritation → squamous dysplasia GORD → Barrett's (squamous→columnar metaplasia) → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma
Treatment Definitive chemoradiotherapy (upper oesophagus — surgically difficult) Neoadjuvant chemo/chemoradio → oesophagectomy
⭐ The two SBA discriminators:
Location: upper/middle = SCC; lower = adeno
Risk factor: alcohol/smoking → SCC; GORD/Barrett's/obesity → adeno
Note: smoking + achalasia raise risk of both types.
Clinical Features
🍽️
Progressive Dysphagia
Solids first → then liquids as lumen narrows. The hallmark. Presentation is typically late — lumen must narrow considerably before symptoms emerge.
⚖️
Weight Loss
Dysphagia + cancer cachexia/anorexia → often profound. A core red flag driving the 2WW pathway.
🗣️
Hoarseness
Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement — implies mediastinal spread. Left RLN most vulnerable.
😣
Odynophagia
Pain on swallowing — ulceration or invasion of surrounding structures.
🔍
Signs of Advanced Disease
Cachexia · Virchow's node (left supraclavicular) · hepatomegaly / jaundice (liver mets) · ascites · Horner's syndrome
💡 Oesophageal cancer lacks symptoms until late → presents advanced → poor prognosis. This is why the ALARM/dyspepsia red-flag pathways emphasise early OGD.
Investigations
Step 1 — Diagnose
🔭
Urgent OGD + Biopsy (2WW)
Any dysphagia at any age, or age ≥55 + weight loss + upper-GI symptom. Biopsy confirms histological type (SCC vs adeno) and grade.
🩻
Barium Swallow
If motility differential considered. Cancer: irregular stricture with shouldering (vs achalasia's smooth "bird's beak").
Step 2 — Stage (Before Treatment)
🖥️
CT Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis + PET-CT
CT for local/regional disease + distant metastases. PET-CT for occult distant mets — refines staging before committing to curative surgery.
🔊
Endoscopic USS (EUS)
T stage (depth of wall penetration) + local nodal involvement. Best tool for local staging — determines surgical resectability.
🔬
Staging Laparoscopy
Junctional (GOJ) tumours only — detects peritoneal metastases not visible on CT/PET.
Management
Curative Intent (MDT-guided)
SCC — Definitive Chemoradiotherapy

Upper oesophagus is surgically difficult (proximity to airway, aorta, RLN). Radical chemoradiotherapy offers equivalent survival to surgery with less morbidity for SCC.

Adeno — Neoadjuvant + Surgery

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy → downstage tumour → oesophagectomy (Ivor-Lewis: right thoracotomy + laparotomy; McKeown: 3-stage). Stomach fashioned into conduit.

Early / High-Grade Barrett's — Endoscopic

Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or radiofrequency ablation (RFA) — avoids major surgery for very early disease or high-grade dysplasia (cross-ref GORD Barrett's section).

Oesophagectomy — Key Points
⚠ Anastomotic Leak

The feared complication. Any post-oesophagectomy patient who deteriorates → assume anastomotic leak until proven otherwise. Presents with sepsis, tachycardia, pleural effusion. High mortality. A classic surgical SBA.

Other Complications / Post-op Care
  • Chest infection / pneumonia — most common complication
  • One-lung ventilation intraoperatively
  • Loss of gastric reservoir → small frequent meals
  • Feeding jejunostomy if swallowing impaired post-op
Palliative Intent (Most Present Too Late for Cure)
🩺
Oesophageal Stent
Self-expanding metal stent to relieve dysphagia. Primary palliation for inoperable disease.
💊
Palliative Chemo / Radio
Tumour shrinkage, bleeding control, pain. Not curative.
🍽️
Nutritional Support
Radiologically inserted gastrostomy (RIG) or nasojejunal tube if unable to swallow. Dietitian involvement essential.
⭐ Exam Pearls
SCC: upper/middle · developing world · smoking/alcohol/achalasia → definitive chemoradiotherapy.
Adeno: lower third · developed world · GORD/Barrett's/obesity → neoadjuvant chemo + oesophagectomy.
Progressive dysphagia (solids→liquids) = cancer until proven otherwise → urgent OGD + biopsy. Achalasia = both simultaneously (motility, not mechanical).
Barrett's → adenocarcinoma (the GORD pathway endpoint). EMR/RFA for early/high-grade Barrett's.
Staging: CT + PET-CT (distant mets) → EUS (T stage/local nodes) → staging laparoscopy (junctional).
Post-oesophagectomy deterioration = anastomotic leak until proven otherwise. Pneumonia is the commonest complication.

UPPER GI__Achalasia:
Overview

Achalasia: failure of lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) relaxation + loss of oesophageal peristalsis → LOS tonically contracted, oesophagus above progressively dilated.

Mechanism: degenerative loss of ganglion cells in Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus → LOS fails to relax on swallowing + absence of coordinated peristalsis throughout the oesophageal body.

⚠ Diagnostic trap: Achalasia mimics both GORD (heartburn, regurgitation) and oesophageal cancer (dysphagia, weight loss). The dysphagia pattern and manometry findings are the key discriminators — see below.
⭐ The Dysphagia Discriminator

The single most testable point — the pattern of dysphagia separates a motility problem from a mechanical obstruction:

Condition Dysphagia pattern Why
Achalasia (motility) Liquids AND solids equally, from the start LOS won't open for anything — pressure problem
Cancer / Stricture (mechanical) Solids first → progresses to liquids Lumen narrows gradually — liquids still pass early
⭐ "Solids then liquids = obstruction (cancer/stricture); both together from the start = motility (achalasia)." This single contrast is a near-guaranteed SBA stem.
Clinical Features
🍽️
Dysphagia
To both solids and liquids equally from the outset — the hallmark. Progressive over months to years.
🔄
Regurgitation
Of undigested food (no acid taste — this is oesophageal, not gastric). Nocturnal aspiration → aspiration pneumonia, chronic cough.
🔥
Heartburn / Chest Pain
Retrosternal discomfort — can closely mimic GORD. A common diagnostic trap.
⚖️
Weight Loss
If severe or long-standing. Raises concern for malignancy — always exclude with OGD.
↑ Oesophageal Cancer Risk
Long-standing stasis → squamous cell carcinoma risk. Small but real malignant transformation risk in untreated achalasia.
Investigations

Diagnostic triad: confirm (manometry) → visualise (barium swallow) → exclude malignancy (OGD)

📊
Oesophageal Manometry
Gold standard / most important test. Shows: excessive LOS tone that fails to relax on swallowing + absent peristalsis in the oesophageal body.
🦜
Barium Swallow
Grossly dilated oesophagus with fluid level + "bird's beak" tapering at LOS. Tertiary contractions → corkscrew appearance.
🔭
OGD (Endoscopy)
Mandatory — exclude malignancy. Specifically rules out pseudoachalasia: a tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction mimicking achalasia. Not optional.
🫁
CXR
Widened mediastinum + air-fluid level behind the heart — the dilated food-filled oesophagus. May be the incidental finding that triggers investigation.
💡 Pseudoachalasia: a GOJ tumour can produce identical manometry findings to true achalasia — OGD + biopsy is the safety step that separates them.
Management

Core logic: all treatments aim to force the LOS open — either mechanically, surgically, or pharmacologically.

🎈
1st Line — Pneumatic (Balloon) Dilatation
Endoscopic balloon mechanically disrupts the LOS muscle fibres. Less invasive than surgery, quicker recovery. Repeat sessions may be needed.
↓ recurrent / persistent symptoms
🔪
Heller Cardiomyotomy — Definitive
Surgical division of the LOS muscle. Often combined with fundoplication (Dor or Toupet) to prevent post-operative GORD from the now-incompetent LOS.
↓ high surgical risk / unfit for surgery
💉
Botulinum Toxin Injection
Intra-sphincteric injection paralyses the LOS. Temporary — effect wears off after months. Reserved for patients unfit for balloon dilatation or surgery.
POEM (Modern Option)

Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy — endoscopic equivalent of surgical myotomy. Tunnels submucosally to divide LOS fibres. Increasingly preferred; comparable efficacy to Heller.

Medical (Temporising Only)

CCBs (nifedipine) or nitrates — reduce LOS pressure. Weak, short-lived effect. Used only as a bridge while awaiting definitive treatment.

⭐ Exam Pearls
Dysphagia to liquids AND solids from the start = achalasia (motility). Solids → then liquids = mechanical obstruction (cancer/stricture).
Mechanism: loss of Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus ganglion cells → LOS fails to relax + absent peristalsis.
Manometry = gold standard (failure of LOS relaxation + absent peristalsis). "Bird's beak" = barium swallow finding.
Always OGD to exclude pseudoachalasia — a GOJ tumour that mimics achalasia exactly on manometry.
Rx ladder: balloon dilatation (1st line) → Heller myotomy (definitive) → botox (unfit). POEM is the modern endoscopic alternative to Heller.
Complications: aspiration pneumonia (nocturnal regurgitation), weight loss, long-term ↑ squamous cell oesophageal cancer risk.
